final_task_tree.title: Figure out a training plan for my dog
final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

1. **Hire, but cheaply.** Leash pulling is a DIY job. The barking-at-dogs part isn't — it's behaviour modification and the risk of doing it wrong is that you make it worse, because the protocols depend on marking within about a second and reading body language before he tips over. No bite history + 14 months = you're just below the "get serious help" line, so the right dose is a class plus one private consult, not a $3,000 programme. Budget $300–800.

2. **Options with real prices** (all pulled from their own sites today):
   - **HSSV "Top Dogs" Level 1 — $300**, six weeks online, and the next cohort starts **Tue 19 Aug at 6:15pm**. This is the standout: reactivity-specific, evening slot, your dog explicitly qualifies, and finishing it unlocks the in-person Level 2 ($300) where he practises around other reactive dogs.
   - **In Tune (Nancy Le)** — consult $195–325, follow-ups $130–215, sliding scale under $115K household income.
   - **Stacy's Wag'N'Train** — most experienced by far, but ⚠️ her site says private and virtual appointments are **weekday daytime only**, which collides with your evenings-and-weekends constraint. Flagged in the calling subtask so you lead with that question.
   - Steered you away from Off Leash K9 San Jose — $500 first lesson bundles an e-collar, wrong tool for a dog barking out of arousal.

3. **Four-week plan** is in the report. The design point worth knowing: the two problems get trained in **separate sessions** — leash work where there are no dogs, reactivity work standing still at distance. Week 1 is foundations with zero dog exposure, weeks 2–3 are engage-disengage (pay him for *looking* first, then for choosing to look *away*), week 4 adds moving dogs and the emergency U-turn. One rule governs all of it: if he won't take food, you're too close.

**Four things now sitting on you**, each with contacts and prices already in the description: register for HSSV (time-sensitive, 19 Aug), email the two trainers, buy the kit, scout two routes. Plus a week-4 checkpoint task with the escalation triggers written into it.

One expectation-setting note I'd rather say plainly: week 4 success is him glancing at you instead of exploding at ~30 feet. It is not him greeting dogs on a pavement. That's month three or four.

report.markdown:
### 1. Hire or DIY?

**Hire — but only a small dose, and combine it with a cheap structured class. Then run the daily work yourself.**

Your dog has two problems that look like one problem, and they aren't the same difficulty:

| Problem | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Pulls hard on leash | **DIY.** A mechanical skill. Well documented, commonly self-taught, no real downside risk to getting it slightly wrong. |
| Barks at every other dog | **Get eyes on it.** Behaviour modification, not obedience. This is the part where DIY commonly backfires. |

**Why the reactivity part warrants help.** The standard threshold for calling a professional is a dog that has bitten or tried to bite, reactivity escalating despite consistent training, severity that makes daily life hard, or an owner who feels out of their depth. A 14-month dog that barks but has no bite history sits just *below* that line — which is why the right dose is a couple of sessions plus a class, not a $3,000 programme.

The specific risk of going it alone is **timing**. The protocols that work here (Look At That, engage–disengage, BAT) depend on marking a behaviour inside about a second and on reading early body language — a stiffening tail, a fixed stare — before the dog goes over. Getting that wrong doesn't merely fail; it can reinforce the reaction or deepen the fear. That's a coaching problem, and coaching is cheap.

Two things are in your favour: 14 months means the habit is months old, not years old, and a border collie mix is about as trainable and food-motivated as dogs come. Prognosis is good.

> ⚠️ The field is unregulated — anyone can call themselves a behaviourist. Filter on **CPDT-KA, CBCC-KA, KPA-CTP, IAABC**. And avoid anyone selling e-collars or prong collars for this: applying pain while your dog is looking at another dog teaches him that other dogs predict pain, which is the exact opposite of the goal.

**Recommended spend: $300–$800.** Book the HSSV class ($300) *and* one private consult (~$200–325). That's the highest-value combination available to you.

---

### 2. Local options, with real prices

All figures published on the providers' own sites, checked 4 Aug 2026.

| | **HSSV "Top Dogs"** ⭐ | **In Tune Dog Training** | **Stacy's Wag'N'Train** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who | Humane Society Silicon Valley, Milpitas | Nancy Le, San Jose | Stacy Braslau-Schneck, San Jose |
| Format | Group course, Level 1 online / Level 2 in person | Private, in-home + remote | Private, in-person or virtual |
| **Price** | **$300 per level** | Consult **$195–$325**, follow-ups **$130–$215** | 6-pack in person **$1,500**; virtual 6-pack **$870**; virtual hourly **$145** |
| Typical total | $300 (L1) or $600 (L1+L2) | ~$845–$1,400 for her recommended 6 sessions | $870–$1,500 |
| Evenings/weekends | ✅ Next cohort **Tue 19 Aug, 6:15pm** | ❓ Ask | ❌ Site says weekday daytime only |
| Contact | dogtraining@hssv.org | (408) 373-1393 · Nancy@intunedogtraining.com | Stacy@wagntrain.com |

**HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 — $300, six weeks, online.** First session 90 min, then five 50-min sessions. Covers threshold work, impulse control, calm exits, emergency exits. Explicitly for dogs 8 months+ who "bark, lunge, or worry" but have not caused injury — your dog qualifies on both counts. Completing it unlocks **Level 2 ($300)**, an in-person class where your dog works around other reactive dogs in a controlled setting. That environment is the single hardest thing to replicate on your own, and $600 for both is remarkable value.
→ Register: https://pro.gofundme.com/event/e826622

**In Tune — best private option.** Force-free, no corrections/choke/prong, explicitly handles reactivity. Offers **sliding-scale pricing for households under $115K/year** — ask. Limits herself to 2–3 clients a day. Serves ~15 miles from the Rose Garden neighbourhood; confirm you're inside it.

**Stacy's Wag'N'Train — most experienced, worst fit for your schedule.** Operating since 1998, force-free, and her top package names leash-reactivity directly. But her site states private *and* virtual appointments are weekdays during the daytime, and she books 2–3 weeks out. Lead with the scheduling question. If she can't do evenings, the virtual 6-pack at $870 is still a real option if you can take a lunch break.

**Avoid:** Off Leash K9 Training of San Jose — $500 first lesson bundles an e-collar. Wrong tool for this dog.

---

### 3. The first four weeks

**Buy first:** front-clip harness · 6ft flat leash (**not** retractable — constant tension makes a loose leash impossible to teach) · waist treat pouch · high-value soft treats (string cheese, hot dog rounds, freeze-dried liver). ~$60–90.

**The one rule that governs everything:** *if he won't take food, you are too close.* That's your threshold, and staying under it is the whole job.

**Never train both problems in the same session.** Leash walking happens where there are no dogs. Reactivity work happens standing still, at distance, not while walking.

Budget ~20 min/day on weekdays in short blocks, plus one 30–45 min weekend session.

#### Week 1 — Foundations, zero dogs
- **Leash (10 min/day, boring street):** the moment the leash goes slack into a J-shape, mark ("yes") and pay at your hip. Tension = you stop dead and wait. Never pull back. Walking forward is itself the reward.
- **Attention (2 min × 3/day, indoors):** say his name, pay the instant he turns. Build this until it's automatic — it's the emergency handle you'll need in week 3.
- **Reactivity: none yet.** Do management only. Cross the road, turn around, use parked cars as visual blocks. Every explosion this week is a rep of the wrong behaviour.
- **Measure and write down:** the furthest-away dog he can see and still eat. That's your week 1 threshold number, and your week 4 checkpoint compares against it.
- **Collie tax:** 10 min/day of sniffing, nose work or puzzle feeding. An under-stimulated collie has a shorter fuse.

#### Week 2 — Engage–Disengage, Level 1
- **Leash:** same, add one turn and one stop-start per walk. Change direction unpredictably so he has to track you.
- **Reactivity (weekend session, plus 1–2 weekday evenings):** park yourself well beyond threshold — 50+ feet, in a car park or on a wide field edge. The instant he *notices* another dog, mark and feed at your hip. **You are paying him for looking, not for ignoring.** 10–20 reps, then leave. Sessions stay short: 5–10 minutes.
- If he fires: you were too close. Move back 10 feet and carry on. No correction, no drama.

#### Week 3 — Engage–Disengage, Level 2 + closing distance
- **Leash:** take it somewhere mildly more interesting — a quiet park path. Expect it to get worse before it gets better. Pay more, not less.
- **Reactivity:** now wait 1–5 seconds after he notices, and mark the moment he **chooses to look away**. This is the whole point — he's learning to self-interrupt. If he stares longer than 5 seconds, you advanced too early; drop back to week 2 for a few more sessions.
- Shave roughly 5 feet off the distance only when he's succeeding at 8 out of 10 reps.

#### Week 4 — Movement, and the checkpoint
- **Leash:** first attempt at a normal route at a quiet hour. Success is a loose leash for stretches, not the whole walk.
- **Reactivity:** introduce *moving* dogs at your working distance — a dog walking past at 40 feet rather than sitting still. Movement raises difficulty sharply, so add distance back when you add it.
- **Emergency U-turn:** teach a cheerful "let's go", pivot, and pay. This is your exit when a dog appears round a corner. Drill it 5 times a day with no dogs present so it works when it matters.
- **Checkpoint:** re-measure the threshold distance and compare to week 1.

#### What week 4 looks like if it's working
He walks past another dog at ~30 feet and glances back at you instead of exploding. **Not** greeting dogs on a narrow pavement — that's month three or four. Four weeks is where the pattern starts, not where it finishes.

**Escalate if:** no change after four consistent weeks, or it worsens → that's "escalating despite consistent training", stop self-directing and get the trainer in. Any contact with another dog or person → skip trainers, go straight to a CBCC-KA behaviour consultant or a veterinary behaviourist.

---

### Do this week
1. **Register for HSSV Top Dogs Level 1** — $300, cohort starts 19 Aug. Time-sensitive.
2. **Email In Tune and Stacy's** about evening/weekend availability.
3. **Buy the harness, leash, pouch and treats.**
4. **Scout two walking routes** — one quiet with long sightlines, one boring with no dogs.

subtasks.title: Decide: hire a trainer vs. DIY for leash pulling + dog reactivity
subtasks.description:
Question 1 of the brief — ANSWERED: hire a trainer for a small number of sessions, then run the plan yourself. Do not go pure DIY, and do not buy a big board-and-train package.

Reasoning:
- The two problems are NOT the same difficulty. Loose-leash walking is a mechanical skill and is very commonly self-taught with good instructions. Barking/lunging at other dogs is an emotional/behaviour-modification problem and is the part where DIY commonly backfires.
- The recognised threshold for "get a pro" is: dog has bitten or tried to bite, reactivity is escalating despite consistent training, severity makes normal daily life hard, or the owner feels out of their depth. (wagbar.com reactivity guide.) A 14-month dog that barks but has no bite history sits just below that line — which is why a few private sessions is the right dose rather than an intensive programme.
- The specific risk of DIY on reactivity is timing. The core protocols (LAT/Look At That, BAT, engage-disengage) depend on marking a behaviour within about a second, and on reading early body-language signals — stiffening, hard stare — before the dog goes over threshold. Getting this wrong doesn't just fail, it can reinforce the reaction or increase fear. (k9academyny.com; sitmeanssit.com.)
- Credentials matter more here than for basic obedience because the field is unregulated — anyone can call themselves a behaviourist regardless of background (AKC). Filter on CPDT-KA / CBCC-KA / KPA-CTP / IAABC.
- Age is in your favour: 14 months is adolescent, the reactivity is recent rather than a decade-long rehearsed habit, and border collie mixes are highly trainable and highly reinforceable. Good prognosis.

RECOMMENDED DOSE: 2-3 private sessions (roughly $400-700 in the South Bay), or one reactivity-specific group course. Private beats group class for session one, because the trainer needs to watch YOUR dog on YOUR street. Then you run the four-week plan and check back in.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS: if the dog ever makes contact with another dog or with a person, skip straight to a CBCC-KA behaviour consultant or a veterinary behaviourist, not a general trainer.

subtasks.title: Build the week-by-week plan for weeks 1-4
subtasks.description:
Question 3 — four-week plan written; full version is in the report attached to the parent task. Design notes and the evidence it rests on:

STRUCTURE: the two problems get trained separately and never in the same session. Loose-leash walking is trained where there are no dogs. Dog-reactivity is trained standing still at distance, not while walking. Mixing them is the most common way owners stall out — you cannot teach a new mechanical skill to a dog that is already over-aroused.

THE THREE RULES THE WHOLE PLAN RESTS ON:
1. Threshold. Threshold is the distance at which your dog starts to react; the entire job is staying under it, so the dog notices the other dog but does not fire. (Blue Ridge Humane; Pawsitively Intrepid.) Practically: find the distance where he can still take a treat. If he won't eat, you are too close — that is the single most useful signal you have.
2. Engage-Disengage. Week 1-2 you mark and pay the moment he LOOKS at the other dog (Level 1). Week 3+ you wait 1-5 seconds and mark the moment he chooses to look AWAY (Level 2). If he stares longer than 5 seconds, you went to Level 2 too early — drop back. (Karen Pryor Clicker Training.)
3. Equipment. Front-clip harness, 6ft flat leash, loose J-shape in the leash. No retractable leashes — they make a loose leash impossible to teach because there is constant tension. No prong or choke collars: they're aversive and, on a dog that already barks at other dogs, they risk pairing pain with the sight of another dog. (Wisconsin Humane; Rover; Dogster.)

TIME BUDGET: ~20 min/day on weekdays split into short blocks, plus one longer 30-45 min weekend session. Deliberately fits evenings and weekends. Short and frequent beats long and rare.

BORDER COLLIE NOTE: a 14-month collie mix that is under-stimulated is a collie mix with a lower reactivity threshold. Sniffing walks and a 10-minute nose-work or puzzle-feeding habit are in the plan not as a nice-to-have but as threshold management.

WHAT SUCCESS AT WEEK 4 ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE — set expectations here: a dog that can walk past another dog at ~30 feet and glance back at you instead of exploding. NOT a dog that can greet other dogs on a narrow sidewalk. That's month three or four. Four weeks is where the pattern starts, not where it finishes.

subtasks.title: Week 4 checkpoint: measure the threshold distance and decide what's next
subtasks.description:
Do this at the end of week 4, before booking anything further.

Measure: stand still on your quiet route and note the closest distance at which your dog can see another dog and still take a treat from you. Compare it to what it was in week 1 (record the week 1 number when you get it).

- Distance has shrunk meaningfully and he's offering to look back at you → the plan is working, keep going, move to weeks 5-8 of the same protocol at closer distances and start adding moving dogs.
- No change after four consistent weeks, or it's got worse → that is exactly the 'escalating despite consistent training' signal that means stop self-directing and get the private trainer in.
- Any contact made with another dog or a person at any point → skip trainers, go to a CBCC-KA behaviour consultant or a veterinary behaviourist.
